Article Title: 'Power Banks' for satellites? Bengaluru Company builds tech to keep ageing spacecraft alive
Article Text:
Aule On-screen setup running multibody dynamics simulations and tracking system capturing hardware test data for position and velocity for correlation

Aule 2: Dark room hardware test setup where the team recreated on-orbit lighting conditions with a sun simulator and a target mounted on a robotic arm to simulate the target’s motion.

BENGALURU: What if satellites could simply plug into a power bank instead of drifting away when they run out of fuel? That’s the idea driving a Bengaluru startup building “jetpack” satellites designed to latch onto ageing spacecraft, take over their propulsion duties and keep billion-dollar assets working years longer.After recently validating a key part of its technology at an Isro facility used for India’s SpaDeX docking mission, Aule Space is now preparing for what could become one of the world’s most ambitious private satellite docking demonstrations.For satellite operators, running out of fuel doesn’t necessarily mean spacecraft have reached the end of life. In many cases, expensive communication satellites remain fully functional, but can no longer maintain their assigned orbital positions because they have exhausted the propellant needed for station-keeping. Once that happens, operators are forced to retire assets worth hundreds of millions of dollars.Aule has found another way. “We’re trying to build satellites which can go and dock to existing satellites in space which don’t have any installed ports... and extend their life so that they can keep generating revenue,” CEO Jay Panchal, told TOI. “It’s like a power bank,” he added.Instead of attempting the far more complicated task of refuelling satellites in orbit, Aule’s approach is to send a smaller “jetpack” spacecraft that docks with an existing communications satellite and assumes responsibility for station-keeping using its own propulsion system.The company plans to target geostationary communication satellites, many of which cost more than $300 million to build and generate significant annual revenues.The challenge lies in docking with satellites that were never designed to be serviced. Rather than relying on dedicated docking ports, Aule will attach its spacecraft to the liquid apogee motor (LAM) nozzle, a standard external feature found on most geostationary satellites.If successful, the technology could help operators extract years of additional service from satellites that would otherwise become orbital relics. Panchal said each docked “jetpack” could extend a satellite’s operational life by up to 5 years.*Key Test Done*The startup recently completed a major milestone by testing its camera-based guidance, navigation and control system at the Rendezvous Simulation Laboratory (RSL) at Isro’s ISITE — the same lab where critical elements of the SpaDeX were validated.“We were the first non-govt entity to access RSL. This is the best kind of on-ground testing we can do for these capabilities,” Panchal said.One of Aule’s differentiators is its reliance on computer vision instead of multiple specialised sensors. Current docking systems typically use LiDAR, infrared cameras and other sensors. Aule says its spacecraft will perform the critical final approach using a single optical camera powered by onboard AI.The visual navigation models are trained using data generated in its own facilities and validated at Isro’s testbed before being deployed in orbit.The company is targeting an in-orbit demonstration next year, when it plans to launch two satellites that will autonomously dock in low-Earth orbit. Panchal claims it could be the world’s first private mission to perform non-cooperative docking in LEO using camera-only navigation. The mission will validate technologies that Aule ultimately intends to deploy around geostationary communication satellites.
Article Summary: Bengaluru startup building ‘jetpack’ satellites designed to latch onto ageing spacecraft. Aule Space preparing for what could become one of the world’s most ambitious private satellite docking demonstrations. Company plans to target geostationary communication satellites, many of which cost more than $300 million to build.

Article Title: IIT-G develops low-cost device to detect toxic metals, bacteria in water
Article Text:
IIT Guwahati researchers develop portable device that quickly detects toxic metals in water

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Researchers at IIT Guwahati have developed a portable optical sensing device that can quickly detect toxic metals, fluoride and bacteria in water samples, offering a low-cost tool for on-site water-quality checks in rural areas and places without easy access to laboratories.Named E-Eye, the device has detected arsenic, lead, iron, chromium, fluoride and Escherichia coli bacteria during laboratory tests, the institute said on Thursday. The estimated cost of the device is about Rs 3,500, with each sample test costing around Rs 2.The device uses a chemical reaction that produces a coloured compound. The intensity of the colour changes according to the concentration of the contaminant. E-Eye analyses the colour through optical sensing, converts the reading into digital data and displays the concentration of the toxicant.According to the researchers, the portable system can be deployed directly at water sources, unlike conventional testing equipment that generally requires samples to be taken to laboratories. It can also wirelessly transmit test results to water-treatment facilities.The team said E-Eye’s results were comparable with those obtained through standard UV-Visible and Atomic Absorption spectrophotometers.More than 2,700 samples have been tested using the device, it added.“The device operates on the Beer-Lambert law and combines optical sensing with digital electronics to generate accurate quantitative measurements. Our device has been able to successfully detect toxicants such as arsenic, lead, iron, chromium, fluoride, and Escherichia coli bacteria,” said Tapas K Mandal, professor in IIT Guwahati’s department of chemical engineering.The researchers said the device could support water-quality monitoring under the Centre’s Jal Jeevan Mission, which seeks to provide tap water to rural households while ensuring that the water supplied is safe.Apart from drinking water, E-Eye can be used to test environmental and biological samples, vegetables, food products, tea, herbal products, soil and milk, the institute said. It may also help industries monitor liquid effluents containing heavy metals, bacteria and odour-causing compounds.The research, supported by a grant from the ministry of electronics and information technology, has been published in the IEEE Sensors Journal. The team includes IIT Guwahati professors Mandal and Harshal B Nemade, along with researchers from the institute, KIIT Bhubaneswar and Ramakrishna Mission Residential College, Kolkata.The researchers have set up ENVIONIX Labs Pvt Ltd to commercialise the technology and are exploring an industry partnership for its transfer. They are also working to integrate solar panels and cloud connectivity into the device for remote monitoring and data management.
Article Summary: IIT Guwahati researchers develop portable device that quickly detects toxic metals in water samples. Called E-Eye, the device has detected arsenic, lead, iron, chromium, fluoride and Escherichia coli bacteria. The estimated cost of the device is about Rs 3,500, with each sample test costing around Rs 2.

Article Title: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's $450 million superyacht hides a secret sea cabin deep inside the hull, designed to reduce seasickness and ensure peaceful sleep during rough voyages
Article Text:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud’s 439-foot Serene one of the most fascinating bedrooms sits three decks below the owner’s suite.

Using naval design to reduce motion

The Balinese inspired cabin. Image – charterworld

Simple Balinese design with practical features

Designer Pascale Reymond once described it as one of the yacht’s coolest ideas (Image – charter​world)

Italian craftsmanship and luxury features

To escape the scorching summer heat of the Middle East, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud equipped his $450 million superyacht Serene with a custom-built snow room cooled to minus 11 degrees Celsius. But despite the yacht's luxurious features, one of its most important design elements is hidden three decks below the main owner's suite.Located near the exact centre of the 439-foot yacht, a secret Balinese-inspired "sea cabin" was specially designed to reduce seasickness and provide a peaceful place to sleep during rough sea journeys.While many billionaire yacht owners place their master bedrooms high up for the best views, Serene has a two-master layout based on how ships move. Reports have long linked the Crown Prince to seasickness during long trips across the Mediterranean and open oceans. Instead of relying only on the yacht's powerful stabilisers, the designers used the science of ship movement to create a calmer sleeping space when the sea becomes rough.The sea cabin is located on the starboard side near the middle of Deck Two, one of the most stable positions on the 134-metre yacht.Naval architecture explains why this location is so effective during voyages. The front of a ship rises and falls heavily in waves, while the rear is affected by pitching, engine vibrations and movement caused by the propellers. Higher decks also move much more from side to side as the yacht rolls.By placing the cabin low in the hull near the centre, the room stays close to the yacht's natural balance points, where movement is at its lowest. Serene is fitted with advanced active stabilisers that greatly reduce rolling, but no system can remove all movement during storms or long ocean crossings. For people who suffer from seasickness, sleeping in the middle of the yacht can make a significant difference.Inside, the sea cabin focuses on calm, simple luxury rather than flashy decoration, creating the feel of a tropical beach retreat. A double bed faces the rear of the yacht beneath a ceiling designed to look like the underside of a traditional Balinese thatched roof. Natural colours, modern furnishings and a floor-to-ceiling headboard separate the bedroom from the open bathroom.One of the cabin's standout features is a large shell door built into the side of the yacht. When Serene is anchored, the door folds down to become a private balcony at sea level, allowing guests to step directly onto the water. During voyages, the balcony stays securely closed, allowing the cabin to serve its main purpose as a stable bedroom.Designer Pascale Reymond once described the cabin as one of the yacht's best ideas because "it's so earthy." Its location is also highly practical. A guest kitchen sits next door, allowing the owner to prepare a late-night snack without calling crew members or climbing several flights of stairs. The spa and beach club are just a short walk away, while a private lift connects the cabin directly to the main owner's suite on Deck Five. This gives the Crown Prince a spacious suite for relaxing in calm waters and a quieter, more stable room for sleeping at sea.Built by Italian shipyard Fincantieri and launched in 2011, Serene is one of the largest and most advanced superyachts ever constructed in Italy. The yacht measures 439 feet (134 metres) long with a beam of 60.7 feet (18.5 metres). Its exterior was designed by Espen Øino, while the interiors were created by Reymond Langton Design. According to Charter World, Serene is powered by eight MTU 4000-series engines, cruises comfortably at 15 knots, reaches a top speed of 20 knots, accommodates 24 guests in 12 cabins, and is operated by a crew of 52.Besides its special sea cabin, Serene offers an impressive range of luxury facilities across seven decks. The yacht has two helicopter landing pads, one of which can be turned into a swimming pool or dance floor, a submarine hangar, and an underwater viewing lounge called the Nemo Room, inspired by Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.To help guests escape the region's extreme heat, the yacht also includes a snow room cooled to around 12 degrees Fahrenheit (-11°C). The room creates real falling snow, allowing guests to move directly into a nearby sauna, hammam, steam room or heated spa pools. With an indoor seawater swimming pool, an outdoor cinema, a piano lounge and domed fireplaces, Serene combines luxury with smart engineering to handle both extreme heat and rough seas.
Article Summary: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud's 439-foot superyacht Serene has a secret Balinese-inspired "sea cabin" The cabin was designed to reduce seasickness and provide a peaceful place to sleep during rough sea journeys. It is located on the starboard side near the middle of Deck Two, one of the most stable positions on the 134-metre yacht.

Article Title: After 27 years and 18 desk moves, Jeff Dean is leaving Google; His ‘goodbye email’ explains why
Article Text:
Jeff Dean, Google's 30th employee and chief scientist, is leaving after 27 years to lead AI startup Discovery Loop.

What Jeff Dean built at Google, and what he wants to build next

Jeff Dean's goodbye email to Google, in full

Subject: Thank you and farewell

Hi everyone,

It has been an absolute pleasure to work with you and to help build some of the most widely used and impactful products of all time. As a kid, I dreamed of helping build software that would be used by many people, and Google now has thirteen products used by more than a billion people (amazing!). Our work has had a tremendous impact in the world, and I have been lucky enough to collaborate and form friendships with many colleagues whom I deeply admire, respect, and enjoy.

It still brings me joy every time I see people out in the world using our products to find information, handle email, translate something, watch videos, learn new things, navigate and understand the physical world, browse the web, use their phone, run large-scale computations on our infrastructure, ride in an autonomous vehicle, or perform complex tasks with the help of our AI systems. I hope you all share this sense of joy, because it is a shared accomplishment!

My longtime friends and collaborators Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le and I have been excitedly discussing how AI can help discover new things with the right kinds of automated loops.

It's a big step, but we've decided to leave Google to co-found Discovery Loop, a new public benefit corporation whose mission is to automate machine learning, science, and engineering to accelerate discoveries and progress.

Ambitious as it sounds, we believe this approach can make meaningful progress against many of the NAE Grand Challenge problems (nae.edu/20782/grand-challenges-project), and we are excited about trying something new, in a smaller setting. Sundar and Alphabet have been very understanding and are helping to support us along with outside investors. We leave with the belief that Google and Gemini are extremely well positioned for amazing impact in the future and we will all be cheering you on from outside!

I have deeply enjoyed collaborating and starting many different kinds of projects here over the last 27 years, and I will miss many aspects of this. Some of the projects and memories I will cherish include:

Working on multiple generations of Google Search as we increased our index size 100X, our queries served / sec 1000X, and our update frequency for the index by 10,000X over a few-year period

Creating the first Google Ads system and later creating and launching Google Content Ads

Helping to launch Google News and Google Translate

Working on infrastructure like MapReduce, BigTable, Spanner, DistBelief, TensorFlow, and Pathways with an awesome set of people

Starting the TPU program and working on other exciting hardware projects with talented colleagues

Doing research with many others on unsupervised learning, model distillation, mixture-of-experts model architectures, word2vec, neural architecture search, RL for ASIC design, AI for health care, and working on multiple generations of Large Language Models (LLMs)

Seeing the awesome work that people in Google Brain and Google Research did over many years when I was lucky enough to manage these organizations

Starting the Gemini effort with Oriol Vinyals as co-tech-leads and working with an amazing team on multiple generations of Gemini and Gemma

Biking to offsites in Monterey

The "Run or Else…" group runs over the last few years

Changing offices 18 times, and visiting 29 Google offices across five continents (did you know that with a Google badge, you can make a cappuccino in more than 100 cities around the world?)

Most importantly, feeling lucky and inspired getting to work amongst such a wonderful and talented group of colleagues

To the many, many people with whom I have worked over the years, I apologize for this impersonal email rather than a face-to-face chat: I didn't want you all to find out through second- or third-hand gossip and it was impractical to tell everyone in a more personal way all at once.

I will be at Google through tomorrow, August 6th. If you're in Mountain View and are so inclined, please stop by my desk and say goodbye in person tomorrow, or drop me a reply to this email. There will be a [remainder redacted in the shared screenshot]

All the best!

-Jeff

Jeff Dean's farewell note to Google runs long, and the most telling part isn't about AI at all. It's a list. Wedged between scaling Google Search's index 100X and starting the TPU program, he mentions biking to offsites in Monterey, a group run called "Run or Else…", changing offices 18 times, and the fact that a Google badge gets you a cappuccino in more than 100 cities. Twenty-seven years, reduced to bullet points he clearly enjoyed writing.The news underneath the nostalgia: Thursday, August 6 is his last day. Dean, chief scientist at Google DeepMind and one of the very few engineers whose work touches nearly every layer of Google's stack, is leaving to co-found Discovery Loop, a public benefit corporation, with Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le. He joined in 1999, when the company had 25 employees. He leaves it at 190,000-plus.CEO Sundar Pichai 's send-off for Jeff Dean drew the same arc: over 27 years, he said, Dean and Ghemawat drove some of Google's most significant technology transitions, from its early search infrastructure to the neural networks that built the modern AI era. "On a personal note, it's been a privilege to work alongside Jeff and Sanjay," Pichai wrote, adding that Google will keep collaborating with the new startup as a founding investor and Cloud partner.Dean’s résumé is most of modern Google. He wrote the first Ads system, helped launch News and Translate, and with Ghemawat designed MapReduce, BigTable and Spanner—systems that became the template for how Amazon and Meta handled global traffic. The two are the only Google employees ever named senior fellow, the company's highest technical honour. Then came 2011 and Google Brain, the research lab Dean built that pushed the entire industry toward AI. Its early hires included Le and Vinyals, the same two men now following him out.That's the quiet irony here. Brain's researchers helped pioneer the technology behind today's chatbots, and Google was slow to act on it. After ChatGPT landed in late 2022, the company folded Brain into DeepMind, and Dean and Vinyals were put on Gemini. His profile inside Google appeared to shrink as Sergey Brin returned and took hold of the AI push.Discovery Loop is an attempt to skip the bureaucracy entirely. The four want to build AI that improves itself with little human input—recursive self-improvement—then point the same machinery at chip design, drug discovery and materials science. Dean's argument is that the experimental loop has always been human-intensive and doesn't have to be. Seed funding comes from Radical Ventures, Khosla Ventures and Alphabet itself, which has also agreed to supply compute for at least a year. It's structured as a public benefit corporation, like Anthropic and OpenAI, and Dean says it may make calls that aren't in the company's purest financial interests.The note ends with an apology for being an email. He didn't want people hearing it as second-hand gossip, he writes, and invites anyone in Mountain View to stop by his desk. That's the tell. A man who spent 27 years building systems for a billion users at a time signed off worrying about how a few thousand colleagues would find out.
Article Summary: Jeff Dean, Google's 30th employee and chief scientist, is leaving after 27 years to lead AI startup Discovery Loop. Dean's goodbye email to Google, in full: "It has been an absolute pleasure to work with you and to help build some of the most widely used and impactful products"

Article Title: Meta launches Muse Code, its first AI coding agent to rival OpenAI and Anthropic
Article Text:
Meta launches Muse Code, its first AI coding agent to rival OpenAI and Anthropic

What is Meta Muse Code and how does it work

Muse Spark 1.2 powers Meta's new coding agent

Meta has launched its first AI coding agent, Muse Code, as the tech giant steps up its push to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic. Currently released in beta, Muse Code is a terminal-based coding agent powered by Meta’s new Muse Spark 1.2 model. Announcing the new models, the company says that it can handle complex software engineering tasks across large code repositories, including planning changes, writing code and checking whether the results work correctly.Unlike a basic AI coding assistant that mainly suggests or generates pieces of code, Muse Code is claimed to be designed to work as an agent capable of carrying out longer and more complicated software engineering tasks. According to Meta, Muse Code uses a main AI agent along with multiple specialised background agents. These background agents remain active throughout a coding session and can gather information, work on next steps and decide when they need to report their findings to the main agent.Meta says this approach can help the coding agent solve difficult problems faster while requiring less intervention from developers.The company says it has also designed Muse Code to handle long-running jobs. Every model call, tool run, approval and code edit is stored in a local event log. If the agent crashes or stops unexpectedly, it can restart from exactly where it left off instead of beginning the task again.Muse Code also comes with built-in skills. The /plan command can create a plan that requires user approval, while /grill can test that plan for possible problems. Another command, /goal, directs the agent to keep working towards completing a specified objective.At the centre of Muse Code is Muse Spark 1.2, Meta's latest AI model and a coding-focused update to Muse Spark 1.1. Meta says it increased the amount of training compute devoted to coding tasks while also expanding the variety of training environments used to develop the new model.The company claims Muse Spark 1.2 improves code generation, complex debugging, understanding of large codebases and end-to-end developer workflows. It has also been trained for long-running coding jobs, including generating entire repositories and working on large projects.
Article Summary: Muse Code is a terminal-based coding agent powered by Meta’s new Muse Spark 1.2 model. It can handle complex software engineering tasks across large code repositories, including planning changes, writing code and checking whether the results work correctly.

Article Title: Twitter product head resigns, sends thanks note to Elon Musk and team; Tesla CEO responds
Article Text:
Nikita Bier thanked Elon Musk and team



Tesla CEO Elon Musk responds to Nikita Bier’s post



Read Nikita Bier’s complete post here



Ladies and gentlemen, it's time to pass the torch and demote myself to my natural state: a poster. I'll be stepping back from leading product for 𝕏 and will continue on as an advisor.

Serving the X community has been the privilege of a lifetime. X is, and will remain, the most important communication technology in history. But running this app is a 24/7 job and it's now time for me to take a breather.

The app is seeing unprecedented growth in new users & engagement. We continue to break records every month. We've climbed 70 spots in the App Store since this time last year.

And in the last 400 days, we rebuilt almost every aspect of X: the Timeline, the Android app, onboarding, notifications, chat and more.

We also launched nearly 30 new products while protecting the integrity of the town square: becoming the first app to show Country-of-Origin on profiles and mounting defenses against AI bots. There's certainly much more work to be done, but our foundation is stronger than ever.

None of this would have been possible without the incredible team here. The next leaders will take X to even greater heights with @benjitaylor on design, @singhai on core product engineering and @dinkin_flickaa on mobile engineering -- among many other great people.

Thank you to Elon and the X team for welcoming me into the company. See you on the Timeline.

Nikita Bier, the product head at X (formerly known as Twitter) has stepped down from his position after serving in the role for just over a year. Bier announced his decision in a post shared on X, saying it was ‘time to pass the torch and demote myself to my natural state: a poster. ’ He added that he will continue to advise the company. Bier, a serial entrepreneur and Lightspeed venture partner, took over the product lead role in July 2025. In his farewell note, he highlighted overseeing the launch of nearly 30 new products and rebuilding core aspects of X, including the timeline, Android app, onboarding, notifications, and chat. He also pointed to record-breaking growth in users and engagement, noting X had climbed 70 spots in the App Store over the past year.His tenure also coincided with controversies, including issues with Grok, the chatbot developed by Musk’s xAI, which was misused to generate harmful content. Despite these challenges, Bier emphasized that X remains “the most important communication technology in history,” but said running the app was a 24/7 job and he needed a breather.Bier expressed gratitude to Elon Musk and the X team, writing: “Serving the X community has been the privilege of a lifetime… None of this would have been possible without the incredible team here.” He named colleagues who will continue leading design, product engineering, and mobile engineering. Musk responded to Bier’s post, thanking him for his contributions.Responding to the goodbye note shared by Bier on X, Tesla CEO Elon Musk thanked him for his contribution. “Thanks for helping make this platform much better! You will be missed,” wrote Musk.
Article Summary: Nikita Bier, product head at X, has stepped down from his role after just over a year. Bier said it was ‘time to pass the torch and demote myself to my natural state: a poster’ Tesla CEO Elon Musk responds to Bier’s post.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Tamil Cinema Embraces Bengaluru Slang, Reflects Evolving Urban Culture
Article Text:
‘Anbe Diana’ incorporates Bengaluru slang to make characters more authentic

The OG bashai boys

J P Chandrababu laid the foundation for Madras bashai in Tamil cinema,

Loose Mohan took that legacy a step further

INDUSTRY SPEAK

Director Pandiraaj:

Geevee Vignesh, showrunner, head of content, Kadhaishorts:





For decades, Tamil cinema relied on polished, literary Tamil or region-specific dialects to establish identity. Madurai had its earthy expressions, Chennai had its ‘Madras bashai,’ and Coimbatore had its Kongu flavour. Today, however, filmmakers are borrowing slang from across India — and social media — to make conversations sound contemporary. The latest entrant is Bengaluru slang, heard prominently in the recently released ‘Anbe Diana’, where characters slip into expressions commonly associated with the city’s multilingual youth culture.It marks an interesting shift in Tamil cinema, where slang is no longer restricted by geography. It has become a storytelling device that reflects migration, urban lifestyles and increasingly blurred linguistic boundaries of southern India. “After ‘Panchathanthiram’ released more than 20 years ago, I felt Tamil cinema had only scratched the surface of the linguistic richness that defines our cities,” says ‘Anbe Diana’ director Pari Elavazhagan . “Chennai is a living mosaic of languages, accents and cultures. People from different parts of the country have made this city their home, each bringing their own dialect, and living in harmony. Neighbourhoods such as Perambur are a celebration of this diversity. Politics may create divisions, but on the streets, people embrace each other’s cultures every single day.” To capture that authenticity, Elavazhagan turned to Bangalore Babu, a 43-year-old who migrated to Chennai more than two decades ago.“Babu didn’t just teach us slang; he introduced us to an entire way of life. We spent hours listening to conversations, understanding the wit, rhythm and cadence of Bengaluru Tamil. Every phrase carries a story, every expression has its own flavour. I wanted the audience to experience that world naturally, not as a gimmick but as a reflection of Chennai’s vibrant multicultural identity,” says Elavazhagan, who got actor Parithabangal Gopi to train with Bangalore Babu. “My character is an admirer of actor Upendra and has strong Bengaluru roots, so getting the slang right was crucial. The learning process was surprisingly quick because I was being taught by people who spoke the slang naturally.”While ‘Anbe Diana’ brought in Bengaluru slang, the ‘Madras bashai’ (Madras slang) revolution came in the early 2000s. Once dismissed as street language, it gained mainstream acceptance through films such as ‘Chennai 600028’, ‘Soodhu Kavvum’, ‘Attakathi’, ‘Madras’ and ‘Vada Chennai’. Words such as ‘macha’, ‘scene’, ‘matter’, ‘local’, ‘mass’ and ‘set aagiduchu’ entered everyday vocabulary across Tamil Nadu. Directors like Pa Ranjith and Vetrimaaran ensured that north Chennai’s dialect wasn’t merely comic relief but an assertion of identity, culture and class.But even before Chennai slang became fashionable, director Bharathiraja had introduced the rustic flavour of southern Tamil Nadu. Between 2005 and 2015, films such as ‘Subramaniapuram’, ‘Paruthiveeran’, ‘Aadukalam’ and ‘Komban’ made Madurai Tamil aspirational. Words such as ‘mapla’, ‘dei maaple’, ‘sarakku’ and countless local idioms travelled beyond the region. The dialect became synonymous with authenticity.‘Anbe Diana’ takes this evolution a step further. Instead of relying solely on Tamil dialects, it reflects the language spoken by thousands of young Tamils living in Bengaluru.The city’s conversations naturally mix Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, English and Hindi. Expressions such as ‘maga’, ‘guru’, ‘bro’, ‘adjust maadi’ and ‘correct agide’ and code-switched sentences have become commonplace among Bengaluru’s youth. By incorporating this speech pattern, the film captures the lived reality of a generation that effortlessly switches languages within a single conversation.The shift also acknowledges the growing movement of Tamil professionals and students to Bengaluru, making the city’s slang instantly relatable for younger audiences.Instagram reels, YouTube creators and meme pages have dramatically shortened the life cycle of slang. A phrase born online today could become a film dialogue tomorrow. Contemporary Tamil films increasingly feature internet-born expressions such as ‘cringe’, ‘bro’, ‘vibe’, ‘toxic’, ‘ghost pannitaan’, ‘simp’, ‘delulu’ and ‘flex’. ‘Adipoli’, a Malayalam slang, has found place in Tamil memes and everyday conversations. Writers are no longer creating slang; they are borrowing it from digital culture.Slang helps establish character within seconds. It instantly conveys a person’s age, background, education, city and social circle. Unlike conventional dialogue, slang also makes films feel current. Audiences often repeat these expressions outside theatres, extending a film’s cultural impact far beyond the screen.The challenge is longevity. Slang evolves rapidly, and what feels trendy today can sound outdated within a year. Excessive dependence on fashionable expressions also risks alienating audiences unfamiliar with those linguistic references.Filmmakers therefore walk a fine line between authenticity and accessibility. The use of Bengaluru slang in ‘Anbe Diana’ signals a larger cultural shift. Tamil cinema is no longer confined to the linguistic identity of Tamil Nadu, but mirrors the lives of Tamils spread across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Dubai, Singapore, London and beyond.Today’s Tamil film dialogue is less about preserving linguistic purity and more about reflecting how people actually speak. In that sense, slang has become more than colourful vocabulary — it has become a marker of identity, mobility and the changing face of modern Tamil culture.making the city’s vibrant street lingo fashionable on screen in the 1950s. With his effortless diction, expressive body language and memorable songs, he transformed what was once considered a working-class dialect into a celebrated cinematic language. Film historians widely credit him with giving Madras bashai its first mainstream identity. His earthy humour, impeccable timing and authentic north Chennai accent made Madras bashai feel natural rather than theatrical. Through hundreds of films, he became synonymous with the dialect, ensuring it remained a staple of Tamil cinema across generations. Together, Chandrababu and Loose Mohan didn’t just speak Madras bashai — they turned it into an enduring cultural signature of Chennai on screenRegional slang was accorded greater importance in the past. A decade ago, filmmakers were more conscious of variations in accents, even across district borders. They prioritised nuances, including the way people addressed their relatives, the tempo of speech, and local linguistic traits. The rise of OTT platforms helped films reach a wider audience across the diaspora. So, the focus has shifted toward making movies accessible and relatable to all Tamils. The intent is to connect with the youth, as they are unlikely to relate to more extreme expressions of regional dialects and slang that resonated with previous generations.In regions such as Coimbatore or Madurai, youngsters do not speak the way their parents did. They adopt a neutral accent and, in many cases, do not embrace their local dialects as strongly as generations before them. Colloquial expressions are not just about authenticity; they help the audience connect with characters and experience their emotions. Even in ‘Parimala and Co’, we had envisioned a family from Trichy. Since we cast Jayaram and Urvashi in the lead, both of whom naturally speak with a Palakkad Tamil accent, we adjusted the narrative to remain authentic to their dialect. It helped preserve realism and allowed audiences to relate to the story.Using a local dialect does more than make a story relatable. It introduces neighbouring communities to forms of Tamil they may rarely hear. Cities that become centres of power move towards a more standardised language, but regional dialects preserve layers of history and culture. For example, the Telugu influence on Chennai Tamil, the traces of Burmese in North Madras speech, the ‘nga’ suffix in Kovai slang. Every slang word carries its own story and plays a part in creating a unique ethnographic soundscape
Article Summary: ‘Anbe Diana’ incorporates Bengaluru slang to make characters more authentic. It marks an interesting shift in Tamil cinema, where slang is no longer restricted by geography. It has become a storytelling device that reflects migration, urban lifestyles and increasingly blurred linguistic boundaries.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Michel Foucault: 'Maybe the target nowadays is not to discover what we are but to refuse what we are' and how every self-help guru got it wrong
Article Text:
Michel Foucault was a French philosopher and historian whose work explored how power, knowledge and social institutions shape human behaviour, identity and society.

"Maybe the target nowadays is not to discover what we are but to refuse what we are."

An essay for a changing world

The Subject and Power

,

How identity is created

Why the idea matters today

The Subject and Power

In 1971, during a televised debate hosted by Dutch philosopher Fons Elders, French philosopher Michel Foucault sat across from linguist Noam Chomsky. Chomsky argued that human beings have a natural, universal human nature that political systems should help develop. Foucault disagreed completely. He argued that what society calls "human nature" is often created by powerful institutions to classify, control and manage people.More than a decade later, Foucault summed up this idea in a single statement:The quote challenges the common belief that people should "find themselves." Instead of looking inward for a true, fixed identity, Foucault argues that many of the labels shaping our identity, including medical diagnoses, gender roles, consumer identities and political categories, are created by society rather than by ourselves. In this view, freedom comes not from discovering a hidden self but from questioning and rejecting the labels placed upon us.The quote comes from Foucault's 1982 essay "" published in the academic journal Critical Inquiry. Written near the end of his life, the essay brings together decades of his research on prisons, psychiatric hospitals, medicine and sexuality.By the early 1980s, Western societies had moved away from the open displays of power seen in earlier centuries.Governments no longer relied mainly on public punishments to control people. Instead, power became quieter and worked through institutions and administration. Foucault argued that modern power mainly operates by shaping individual identity. Institutions tell people who they are, whether as a patient, a criminal, a consumer or a productive worker.Writing for political theorists and social scientists, Foucault argued that the biggest struggle of the modern age was no longer only against religion or economic inequality. It was also against systems of power that define people's identities and expect both individuals and society to accept those identities as truth.The quote is correctly attributed to Foucault. The Subject and Power remains one of his most widely cited works and explains many of his later ideas about power and resistance.To understand Foucault's philosophy, it is important to understand his idea of "subjectification" (assujettissement). In French, the word has two meanings. It describes becoming an independent individual while also becoming controlled by others.Since the Enlightenment, many Western philosophers believed that discovering the truth about yourself leads to freedom. René Descartes searched for certainty through the thinking mind, while Sigmund Freud explored the unconscious to understand human behaviour. Foucault challenged this tradition. He argued that when people receive psychological diagnoses, attend therapy or complete surveys, they are taking part in systems that define what is considered normal and abnormal.In Foucault's view, knowledge and power cannot be separated. When medicine defines mental health, or economics defines a successful citizen, those definitions also create social boundaries. People then begin to judge themselves according to those standards.Refusing what we are becomes a way of resisting these institutional limits. Instead of asking, "Who am I?", Foucault asks, "How has society shaped who I am, and how can I move beyond those limits?" His thinking builds on Immanuel Kant's idea that people should think for themselves. It also adds another challenge. We should question the ideas and categories that society gives us.More than four decades after Foucault wrote, his ideas seem especially relevant in today's digital world.In 2026, technology companies and artificial intelligence systems collect huge amounts of personal data. Algorithms study browsing history, location, typing habits and shopping behaviour to build detailed profiles of each user. These systems predict what people will buy, what opinions they may hold and even which communities they belong to. Social media often rewards people for fitting into these digital identities, creating echo chambers that reinforce them.When people accept these algorithm-created profiles as their true identity, they reflect the concern Foucault raised. Applying his ideas today means questioning these categories instead of simply accepting them. It may mean rejecting a workplace culture that measures personal worth only through productivity, or treating a mental health diagnosis as a useful medical tool instead of allowing it to become a person's entire identity.For Foucault, refusing an imposed identity is not about withdrawing from society. It is an active choice to resist allowing institutions to decide what a person's life should be.Foucault never offered a perfect vision of what people should become after rejecting these labels. Instead, he believed freedom is an ongoing process of questioning the identities and definitions handed down by authority while creating space to live beyond them.
Article Summary: Michel Foucault was a French philosopher and historian. His work explored how power, knowledge and social institutions shape human behaviour, identity and society. He argued that what society calls "human nature" is often created by powerful institutions to classify, control and manage people. His ideas seem especially relevant in today's digital world.

Article Title: A 45,000-year-old crystal tool found in France suggests Neanderthals chose beauty as well as practicality
Article Text:
A remarkable find in France reveals a 45,000-year-old Neanderthal quartz scraper that changes the narrative around these ancient beings. This tool, crafted from rare rock crystal, highlights that Neanderthals had an appreciation for aesthetics and craftsmanship, challenging the notion of them as mere primitive beings. The sophistication in its creation suggests a deeper cultural understanding and skillful manipulation of their environment, offering insights into Neanderthal life and artistry.

45,000-year-old Neanderthal quartz scraper highlights unusual stone tool technology in France

Neanderthal rock crystal tools show careful material selection

PC: Ministère de la Culture

Neanderthal creativity beyond old stereotypes

Ancient tool revealed the complexity of Neanderthal culture

A small artefact with a long scientific legacy

A small piece of translucent quartz discovered in a French cave nearly a century ago has continued to reshape the way scientists view Neanderthals. The object, a carefully worked rock crystal scraper, was not made from the materials these prehistoric toolmakers usually relied upon. Instead, someone selected a rare, visually striking stone and transformed it into a practical tool. Its careful manufacture has prompted archaeologists to reconsider how Neanderthals chose raw materials and whether appearance influenced certain tool-making decisions. Found among other quartz artefacts in the Dordogne region, the discovery challenged early assumptions that Neanderthals lacked creativity or an appreciation for unusual materials. Today, the artefact offers a glimpse into how function and visual appeal may have existed together in Neanderthal craftsmanship.The rock crystal scraper comes from Abri des Merveilles, an archaeological site in southwestern France’s Dordogne region. Reportedly, the cave became significant after American archaeologists uncovered a group of unusual quartz tools there in 1924.As per the 1931 American School of Prehistoric Research bulletin , the excavation was led by George MacCurdy from the institution now associated with Harvard University.Among the finds was a transparent, yellow-tinted piece of microcrystalline quartz that had been shaped into a tool. The artefact is now held by France’s National Archaeological Museum.Unlike many Neanderthal tools made from flint or chert, this object was created from rock crystal, a material that behaves differently when fractured. Flint was often preferred because it produced predictable sharp edges, making it reliable for cutting and scraping tasks. Quartz required more skill and judgement, as its structure made shaping it less straightforward.The cave also contained small fragments of quartz left behind during production, suggesting the tool was likely made at the site rather than carried there after completion.The presence of rock crystal tools at Neanderthal sites has long attracted attention because the material appears to have been selected for more than just its usefulness.The scraper may have served a practical purpose, possibly as a combination scraping and pointed implement. Yet its clear appearance and unusual colour raised questions about why Neanderthals chose this stone when other materials were easier to work.According to Harvard University, American School of Prehistoric Research, the quartz may have come from deposits connected to waterways near the Vézère River, a tributary of the Dordogne. The exact age of the Abri des Merveilles layers remains uncertain, but archaeological evidence suggests the tools were created somewhere around 45,000 years ago.For much of the early 20th century, Neanderthals were often portrayed as primitive and lacking the abilities associated with modern humans. According to the 1931 bulletin, these ideas were heavily influenced by interpretations of Neanderthal fossils, including the remains of an elderly individual from La Chapelle-aux-Saints in France.The individual had suffered from severe arthritis, but early interpretations focused on physical differences and helped create the inaccurate image of Neanderthals as crude, almost animal-like beings.MacCurdy’s interpretation of the rock crystal tools offered a different perspective. He argued that the choice of material showed an awareness of shape, colour and quality. In his view, the tools indicated that Neanderthals were capable of recognising aesthetic qualities even while making objects for everyday use.He did not describe them as artists in the same way as later human societies are understood to have been, but he suggested that they possessed a sense of visual appreciation.When the quartz tools were first studied, evidence of Neanderthal symbolic behaviour was far more limited than it is today. Archaeologists had not yet uncovered many of the examples now associated with Neanderthal creativity, including possible pigment use, engravings and decorative objects.Later discoveries and advances in genetics changed the scientific picture of Neanderthals. Evidence that they interbred with Homo sapiens, along with growing research into their behaviour, has shown that they were far more complex than earlier descriptions suggested.The rock crystal scraper became an early piece of evidence in that shift. It showed that Neanderthal technology was not simply about survival and efficiency, but could also involve decisions influenced by the appearance and character of materials.The Abri des Merveilles scraper remains a modest object in size, but its importance lies in the questions it raised. A single quartz tool forced archaeologists to reconsider assumptions about the minds behind prehistoric technology.The artefact’s careful shaping and unusual material choice provide a rare connection to the decisions of an individual Neanderthal craftsman thousands of years ago. Whether the stone was selected partly because of its beauty or simply because it was available, its existence shows that Neanderthal toolmaking involved thought, preference and a close relationship with the materials around them.Nearly 45,000 years later, the small piece of rock crystal continues to offer evidence of a more nuanced understanding of one of humanity’s closest extinct relatives.
Article Summary: 45,000-year-old Neanderthal quartz scraper highlights unusual stone tool technology in France. Tool, crafted from rare rock crystal, highlights that Neanderthals had an appreciation for aesthetics and craftsmanship. The sophistication in its creation suggests a deeper cultural understanding of their environment.

Article Title: The 'Caspian Sea Monster': How a Cold War spy satellite uncovered a mysterious 100-metre Soviet craft unlike any aircraft ever built
Article Text:
Image: CNN

Why the Soviet Union built an entirely new type of vehicle

How the 'Caspian Sea Monster' challenged the rules of aviation

From Cold War experiment to missile carrying sea monster

Why the revolutionary concept never became mainstream

A Cold War mystery that still fascinates engineers today

In the 1960s, as the United States and the Soviet Union competed for technological and military dominance during the Cold War, American spy satellites photographed something extraordinary along the shores of the Caspian Sea. Stretching almost 100 metres in length, the enormous craft appeared far too large to be a conventional aircraft, yet intelligence analysts observed it travelling rapidly across the water. Its unusual shape defied easy classification, it looked neither like a ship nor an aeroplane.Unable to identify the mysterious machine, US intelligence gave it the nickname "Caspian Sea Monster." For years, the discovery fuelled speculation that the Soviet Union had developed a revolutionary military technology capable of changing naval warfare. The truth turned out to be just as remarkable: it was neither a traditional aircraft nor a conventional vessel, but a giant ekranoplan, a craft that flew using an unusual aerodynamic principle known as ground effect.The mysterious machine was eventually identified as the KM ekranoplan, an experimental wing-in-ground-effect (WIG) vehicle developed by the Soviet Union's Central Hydrofoil Design Bureau. Rather than flying at high altitudes like an aeroplane, the ekranoplan skimmed only a few metres above the water by exploiting an aerodynamic phenomenon known as ground effect.When a wing flies extremely close to a flat surface, air becomes compressed beneath it, creating additional lift while reducing drag. This cushion of compressed air allowed the enormous craft to travel at aircraft-like speeds while carrying payloads more commonly associated with ships.According to the US Naval Institute, Soviet engineers spent decades developing multiple WIG prototypes from the 1960s through the early 1990s. They believed these unusual vehicles could combine the speed of aircraft with the cargo capacity of ships while operating entirely from the water.The KM was unlike anything that had existed before. Measuring approximately 92 metres long and powered by ten turbojet engines, it became one of the largest flying machines ever constructed. Yet many engineers hesitate to classify it as a true aircraft because it depended on remaining within ground effect, typically flying only a few metres above the sea.Its unusual operating characteristics offered several military advantages. Flying so close to the water meant it remained below much of conventional radar coverage while travelling far faster than traditional naval vessels. It could transport troops, equipment and supplies across vast stretches of water without relying on ports or runways.This combination of speed, carrying capacity and low-altitude operation convinced Soviet planners that ekranoplans could become valuable military transport platforms, especially across enclosed seas such as the Caspian and Black Seas.The success of the original KM prototype encouraged Soviet engineers to build several other ground-effect vehicles. Among the best known was the Lun-class ekranoplan, designed to carry anti-ship missiles, while the A-90 Orlyonok served as a military transport capable of moving troops and equipment rapidly across coastal waters.The US Naval Institute notes that these vehicles were intended for a variety of missions rather than a single role. Their ability to move at aircraft speeds while carrying ship-like loads made them attractive for military logistics, amphibious operations and rapid transport. Soviet planners viewed them as a unique capability that neither conventional aircraft nor ships could fully replicate.Despite their remarkable engineering, ekranoplans also faced significant operational challenges. Because they relied on ground effect, they performed best over relatively calm water and had limited ability to operate in rough seas or over mountainous terrain. They also required specialised maintenance and infrastructure, making them less versatile than conventional aircraft.Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, funding for ekranoplan development largely disappeared, and most programmes were abandoned before they could enter widespread service.Interestingly, the concept has never completely vanished. Advances in modern materials, logistics requirements and military strategy could make wing-in-ground-effect vehicles relevant once again. They suggest that future WIG craft could complement traditional aircraft and ships by transporting heavy payloads rapidly without depending on vulnerable runways or large ports.What first appeared in grainy satellite photographs as an unidentified Soviet superweapon ultimately became one of the most ambitious engineering experiments of the twentieth century. The Caspian Sea Monster blurred the line between aircraft and ships, forcing engineers to rethink how heavy vehicles could move across vast bodies of water.More than half a century after it startled American intelligence analysts, the giant ekranoplan remains a symbol of Cold War innovation and experimentation. It demonstrated that exploiting the physics of ground effect could create an entirely new class of vehicle, one that challenged conventional definitions of flight and continues to inspire military planners and aerospace engineers today.
Article Summary: The KM ekranoplan was an experimental wing-in-ground-effect (WIG) vehicle. Soviet engineers spent decades developing multiple WIG prototypes from the 1960s through the early 1990s. They believed they could combine the speed of aircraft with the cargo capacity of ships while operating entirely from the water.

Article Title: In 2020, Boston introduced a floating wetland in the Charles River to test whether plant roots could help curb algal blooms
Article Text:
Boston is pioneering floating wetlands to elevate the ecological condition of the Charles River. These ingenious platforms harness plant roots to filter out nutrients from urban runoff, significantly aiming to diminish algal blooms and promote healthy habitats for wildlife. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

How a floating garden works beneath the river's surface

A team of researchers will evaluate the wetlands' performance over several years and seasons, contributing to extensive goals of reviving the river's overall health and enriching its biodiversity. Image Credits: Instagram/@Charles River Conservancy

A research study for developing innovative methods to improve the river’s health

Cities are looking for ways to improve river health without relying only on large-scale engineering projects. In Boston, one nature-based experiment is testing whether plants can help offer that solution. In 2020, a floating wetland was introduced into the Charles River as part of The Charles River Floating Wetlands Project , creating a living platform where native vegetation grows above the water while an extensive network of roots develops below the surface.The installation is part of The Charles River Floating Wetlands Project, which is testing whether floating wetlands can reduce nutrient pollution, limit algal blooms and create habitat for wildlife in an urban river. Rather than presenting the approach as a complete answer to water quality challenges, the project is examining how it could support broader restoration efforts already taking place in the Charles River.The floating wetland resembles a small island of plants drifting on the water. Most of the action happens below the surface, where the roots create an underwater environment that supports a variety of natural processes.The Charles River Floating Wetlands Project explains that the wetland is built on a buoyant structure planted with native wetland species. As the vegetation grows, long roots extend into the river, increasing the amount of submerged surface available for naturally occurring bacteria and other microorganisms to colonise.These microscopic communities play an important role in the ecosystem. According to the project, they interact with nutrients dissolved in the water and may help absorb or transform excess nitrogen and phosphorus that contribute to algal blooms. Researchers are studying this process under real river conditions to better understand how much floating wetlands can contribute to improving water quality over time.Nitrogen and phosphorus enter rivers from a range of urban sources. Stormwater runoff can carry fertilisers, pet waste and other pollutants into waterways, particularly after heavy rainfall. When these nutrients accumulate, they encourage rapid algae growth. Large algal blooms can reduce water clarity and, in some situations, lower the amount of oxygen available for fish and other aquatic life.The project says the dense underwater roots can provide shelter for fish, aquatic insects and other small aquatic organisms. In waterways where urban development has reduced natural wetlands, floating vegetation may help restore some lost habitat.The initiative also highlights the flexibility of the floating design. Because the wetlands float on the water's surface, they can be installed without extensive excavation or major changes to the riverbed. That lets researchers observe how the wetlands perform while minimising disturbance to the surrounding environment.Native plants were selected because they are suited to local conditions. Their ability to tolerate seasonal weather patterns makes them suitable for long-term monitoring, while their growth gradually expands the underwater root network that supports microbial activity.The floating wetland introduced in 2020 serves as a research and demonstration site rather than a permanent solution. The Charles River Floating Wetlands Project is monitoring how the plants establish themselves, how the underwater root systems develop and how the surrounding ecosystem responds over time. Seasonal factors such as water temperature, rainfall, river flow and plant growth can all influence the performance of the floating wetland, making long-term observation an important part of the study.The floating wetland introduced in 2020 serves as a research and demonstration site, not a permanent fix. Scientists are monitoring plant establishment, root development and the effects of seasonal changes on the surrounding ecosystem. Water temperature, rainfall, river flow and plant growth can all affect how the wetlands perform, which is why observations over several years are considered important.In many cities, creating new wetlands along riverbanks is difficult because land is already taken up by roads, buildings and public spaces. Floating wetlands offer a different option by introducing vegetation directly onto the water without requiring additional riverside land.Beyond their environmental role, the floating wetlands also make the research easier for the public to see. People walking, cycling or boating along the Charles River can spot the planted platforms and learn more about the challenges facing urban waterways and the approaches being explored to address them.The Charles River Floating Wetlands Project emphasises that floating wetlands are only one part of a wider strategy for improving river health. Reducing nutrient pollution still depends on measures that keep contaminants out of the water, including effective stormwater management and long-term restoration efforts. The floating wetlands are being evaluated as a complementary approach that could support these broader initiatives.Through the process of studying the relationship between the native flora, naturally occurring microbes, and the changing environment, the experiment hopes to establish knowledge on where this method would be most suitable. This would be beneficial for future projects that intend to restore water bodies in other cities while at the same time conserving local wildlife.
Article Summary: Boston is pioneering floating wetlands to elevate the ecological condition of the Charles River. These ingenious platforms harness plant roots to filter out nutrients from urban runoff, significantly aiming to diminish algal blooms and promote healthy habitats for wildlife. The Charles River Floating Wetlands Project is monitoring how the plants establish themselves, how the underwater root systems develop and how the surrounding ecosystem responds.

Article Title: Quote of the day by JS Mill: 'I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than...' and the 19th-century cure for modern burnout
Article Text:
John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind

I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than in attempting to satisfy them.”

The breakdown of a calculating mind

The utilitarian paradox

Curbing the engine of infinite wants

A shopper standing in the middle of a brightly lit superstore, holding three slightly different versions of the same household item, often feels an odd sense of confusion rather than freedom. The endless scroll of online stores promises that the perfect product to complete life is just one click away. Yet, as packages keep arriving at the door, the promised happiness often disappears, replaced by a lingering desire for whatever comes next.This cycle of endless consumption is exactly what the Victorian philosopher John Stuart Mill described when he wrote: “Mill’s observation completely changes the usual idea of finding happiness. Instead of seeing human desire as an endless list of needs that must be fulfilled, he argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Satisfaction, in his view, does not come from building a bigger net to catch every passing impulse, but from reducing what we expect and demand from the world.John Stuart Mill published this reflection in his Autobiography in 1873, a book describing one of the most intense intellectual upbringings in Western history.Born in London in 1806, Mill was raised under a strict educational experiment designed by his father, James Mill, and the founder of Utilitarianism, Jeremy Bentham. By the age of three, he was learning Ancient Greek; by eight, he was reading Herodotus and Plato in their original language; and by his early teens, he had mastered political economy and formal logic.The purpose of this education was to create a perfectly rational follower of Bentham—a person trained to judge every action by calculating how to produce the greatest pleasure and the least pain for the greatest number of people.The experiment seemed successful until 1826, when twenty-year-old Mill suffered a serious mental breakdown. In one of the most famous parts of his memoir, Mill recalled asking himself a simple question: if all his political and social goals were achieved tomorrow, would he truly feel happy? His honest answer was an immediate “no.” His highly rational way of thinking had left him emotionally empty.Mill’s recovery happened gradually, helped by the poetry of William Wordsworth and by a major reconsideration of Utilitarian philosophy. He realized that Bentham’s basic idea—treating happiness as simply the total of fulfilled desires—was deeply incomplete. To recover his peace of mind, Mill had to rethink what true well-being meant. The quotation from his Autobiography marks this important turning point, showing his realization that lasting happiness comes from controlling desire rather than satisfying every new craving.To understand Mill’s change in thinking, we must examine a tension within Utilitarian philosophy. Traditional Utilitarianism viewed happiness as the total amount of pleasure minus pain. If people could continue creating and satisfying new desires, happiness should, in theory, continue increasing.Mill recognized the major problem with this idea: human desires constantly grow. As soon as one desire is fulfilled, our expectations rise again, a pattern that modern psychologists call the “hedonic treadmill.” Trying to find lasting happiness by satisfying every new want is like trying to fill a bucket full of holes.By encouraging people to limit their desires, Mill was not promoting extreme self-denial or the lifestyle of monks. Instead, he brought his updated version of Utilitarianism closer to older philosophical traditions. Epicurus had argued centuries earlier that simple, easily achieved pleasures bring the greatest peace of mind, while Stoic thinkers such as Seneca believed that true wealth comes not from owning many things, but from wanting fewer things.Mill adapted this idea for the modern industrial world. He argued that higher intellectual and emotional pleasures—such as art, friendship, public service, and personal development—are naturally more valuable than endlessly collecting material possessions. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness that do not lose their value once they are achieved.In 2026, Mill’s insight speaks directly to one of the biggest challenges of modern life: the commercialization of human attention and desire. Today’s digital systems are carefully designed to constantly create new wants that can only be satisfied through more consumption. Targeted algorithms, personalized advertising, and micro-influencers work together to convince people that something important is always missing from their lives.The growing popularity of voluntary simplicity, digital minimalism, and anti-consumption movements reflects Mill’s principle in action. When technology workers switch to basic feature phones or consumers commit to “no-buy” years, they are putting his idea into practice. They are not doing so because they lack money, but because they want to break the endless cycle of constantly creating new desires.The same principle also applies to work and professional burnout. Modern workplaces often define success through constant growth: higher salaries, bigger teams, and continuous promotions. However, research in behavioral economics consistently shows that once people reach a comfortable middle-class standard of living, extra income brings smaller and smaller increases in everyday happiness. Executives who reject promotions to protect their personal lives or professionals who choose lower-paying jobs for better health are deciding to reduce their ambitions rather than spend their lives chasing ever-growing demands.By describing happiness as the relationship between what people have and what they want, Mill offered a lasting mathematical insight: the result can be improved either by increasing what you have or by reducing what you want.When Mill died in Avignon in 1873, he left behind writings that influenced modern liberal democracy, individual freedom, and economic thought. Yet perhaps his greatest personal achievement was overcoming the crisis of his youth. By understanding that peace of mind depends on controlling desire instead of constantly feeding it, he left a timeless guide for staying mentally balanced in a world designed to keep people forever wanting more.
Article Summary: John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind. He argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness.
